title: Highlights from Stanford's AI+Education Summit
author: Dan Meyer
summary: Dan Meyer reports from Stanford's AI+Education Summit, arguing that the field's mood has shifted from 2023's AI triumphalism toward a more sober reckoning with the technology's risks. He highlights Stanford researcher Guilherme Lichand's study finding that middle-schoolers who used an AI creativity tool with guardrails did better in the short term but worse once the tool was removed, with a transfer task revealing a fourfold negative effect concentrated in students who came to believe AI was more creative than they were. Teacher Michael Taubman's remark that "the classroom is taking on an almost sacred dimension" for him captures a recurring theme: panelists kept returning to the value of shared human space even as AI tools become available. Venture capitalist Miriam Rivera used her time to warn about a resurfacing belief in Silicon Valley that some people are simply "better" than others, and about how segregated by class and education level many AI builders' social worlds have become. In a closing debate, former Stanford president John Hennessy pushed panelists to explain why AI's promise should be taken more seriously than the MOOC revolution's promise a decade earlier. Meyer closes skeptically, arguing that AI tutors will fall short for the same reason MOOCs did: it's humans who help humans do hard things, and technologies that isolate a student with a machine tend to underperform regardless of the model behind them.
points: Stanford's Guilherme Lichand found that AI-assisted creative gains for middle-schoolers reversed once the tool was removed, with a transfer task showing a fourfold negative effect concentrated among students who came to believe the AI was more creative than they were.

Teacher Michael Taubman's line that "the classroom is taking on an almost sacred dimension" reframes AI-era teaching as protecting a human space for growing up together, not just delivering content more efficiently.

Venture capitalist Miriam Rivera's warning about resurfacing eugenics-adjacent beliefs in Silicon Valley, and the class/education segregation among AI's builders, complicates the summit's optimism about AI expanding opportunity.

Meyer frames the summit's mood shift bluntly -- "the party is sobering up" -- with panelists now expecting AI's learning gains to be contingent on local implementation and just as likely to produce learning losses.

Meyer's closing argument is that AI tutors will fail for the same structural reason MOOCs failed a decade earlier -- technologies that put a student in an "airtight container" alone with a machine, cut off from other humans, underperform regardless of the model inside them.
quotes: The triumphalism of 2023 is out. The edtech rapture is no longer just one more model release away. Instead, from the first slide of the Summit above, panelists frequently argued that any learning gains from AI will be contingent on local implementation and just as likely to result in learning losses.

It's not just persistence. It's a little bit about how you don't have as much fun doing it, but most importantly, you start thinking that AI is more creative than you. And the negative effects are concentrated on those kids who really think that AI became more creative than them.

In the last year or so, it's really started to feel like we have 45 minutes together and the together part is what's really mattering now. We can have screens involved. We can use AI. We should sometimes. But that is a human space. The classroom is taking on an almost sacred dimension for me now.

Silicon Valley has had a long history of really anti-social kinds of movements including in the earliest days of the semi-conductor, a real belief that there are just different classes of humans and some of them are better than others. I can see that happening with some of the technology champions in AI.

I think for many of us and our students here, that is the world that they primarily inhabit, and they have very little exposure to the real world and to the real needs of a lot of Americans, the majority of whom are in financial situations that don't allow them to have a $400 emergency.

Look -- this is more or less how the same crowd talked about MOOCs ten years ago. Copy and paste. And AI tutors will fall short of the same bar for the same reason MOOCs did: it's humans who help humans do hard things.

And so many of these technologies -- by accident or design -- fit a bell jar around the student. They put the kid into an airtight container with the technology inside and every other human outside. That's all you need to know about their odds of success.
